Good Night (1964).

Director: Rainer Werner Fassbinder.
Writer: Rainer Werner Fassbinder.

After the initial scenes introducing the two friends Arno, a German engineer with some dark past which he prefers to keep under control, a black market dealer selling everything on the corner on Mitterand. The story builds slowly, to show the evolution of this relationship and friendship that they had a few years earlier; that was when the film moves towards some more intense emotion.

Arno has been keeping in touch the couple, through letters, but he is not ready to face directly the truth yet.

The camera work during his visits shows how the place they used and where he used to have fun has changed. Not because they are not there, but he changed, because something in his mind changed, and maybe all is part of a more complicated issue, that's hard to figure right at the beginning.

As the film gets darker, one has to figure who's going to come out of it as a clear winner. And even if there is a clear choice, which will probably depend a lot from the spectator's taste,

, a part stays uncertain until you see the very end.

An intriguing portrait on human relations and emotions

which is not for a wide audience; but those that do want to see films as real-life's moments and events should not miss it. This is the way a director makes you feel with his films and you never know how it will affect your feelings, your thoughts or your behavior.
